subject: Performance benchmarking methodology and evidence for RFP - Peregrine Health
messages:
From: Alex Jones <alex.jones@peregrinehealth.com>
To: Hannah Schmitt <hannah.schmitt@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-07-26T09:15:00-07:00
Subject: RFP - Appendix C: performance test clarifications

Hannah,

Thanks for the quick turn on the RFP so far. We reviewed Appendix C and have a few clarifications before we circulate to our engineering review board:

1) Can you describe the exact synthetic load methodology you used to produce the p50/p95/p99 numbers in the spreadsheet? Specifically: traffic mix (sync vs async), average token length, and warm vs cold-start handling.

2) How do you measure end-to-end latency for chat flows that include tool calls (external API fetch) and is that included in the numbers you provided?

3) For multi-tenant hosted customers, what isolation guarantees are in place so our workload doesn't see noisy neighbors during peak burst events?

4) If a model variant drops (OOM / infra), what automatic fallback behaviors do you offer and how are they reflected in SLA calculations?

We need a short written response and any test artifacts (raw CSV exports, synthetic generator config, and a short runbook) by EOD Tuesday so we can include it in the vendor comparison packet. Procurement will want any explicit assumptions called out.

Attached: Peregrine_RFP_Appendix_C_performance.xlsx (the copy we received)

Best,
Alex
Alex Jones
Director, Platform Engineering
Peregrine Health

From: Hannah Schmitt <hannah.schmitt@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Jones <alex.jones@peregrinehealth.com>
Cc: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-07-26T12:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: RFP - Appendix C: performance test clarifications

Alex — thanks for the clear list. We're happy to provide an itemized response plus artifacts. I've attached an initial bundle with our summary table and a compact evidence tarball. Jonas (SE) is copied — he'll share the detailed test plan and generator configs. Marissa (perf engineer) will follow with the raw CSVs and the latency matrix.

High-level notes up front so procurement has context:
- Our p50/p95/p99 are measured as server-side token generation latency (inference step) under controlled synthetic traffic. They exclude external tool call latency unless explicitly noted.
- Tests include both steady-state sustained QPS and burst phases; we report warm-state metrics after prefix-KV priming to reflect realistic ongoing sessions.
- For multi-tenant hosted, we provide capacity reservations and soft isolation via scheduling + hard isolation for Dedicated. Tenant contention is modeled in our load tests; details below.

Attachments: redwood_perf_evidence_v1.tar.gz (summary + sample CSVs)

I'll leave the technical deep-dive to Jonas and Marissa; please flag any follow-ups after you read.

—Hannah
Hannah Schmitt
Senior Director, Solutions
Redwood Inference

From: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Jones <alex.jones@peregrinehealth.com>
Cc: Hannah Schmitt <hannah.schmitt@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-07-27T08:30:00-07:00
Subject: Re: RFP - Appendix C: performance test clarifications

Alex — thanks, below is the test methodology and the concrete metrics mapping. I'll attach the generator config (inference_test_plan.md) and a short checklist you can hand to your SREs.

Test methodology summary:
- Workloads: We ran three synthetic profiles designed to mimic (a) chat-short (avg prompt 32 tokens, completion 16 tokens), (b) chat-med (avg prompt 80 tokens, completion 64 tokens), (c) long-form (avg prompt 256 tokens, completion 512 tokens). Each profile has a 20%/10%/70% split in a baseline run and we also test single-profile extremes for stress.
- Load driver: custom k6 + async request feeder that dispatches requests with realistic think times and supports session-affinity to exercise prefix/KV cache behavior. Config files included.
- Latency definitions:
  * token-generation latency: time between model receive step for token N and token N+1 emitted from GPU pipeline (server-side).
  * response latency (end-to-end within Redwood): request receive -> final chunk emitted (excludes downstream external tool calls).
  * observed client tail: includes network + chunking; we provide separate CSVs so you can correlate.
- Warm vs cold: cold-start measured from VM/worker spin-up + model load (we list cold timeouts). Warm-state metrics reported after a priming phase where a representative set of prefixes is sent to populate KV caches across replicas (we run the priming for 10 minutes prior to steady-state).
- Concurrency and batching: we test at QPS targets of 50, 250, 1k, 5k for endpoints configured with 1/4/16 replicas respectively. Batching window is set to 15ms by default (configurable). For each QPS we measure throughput, average batch size, and tail latency.

SLO mapping and graceful degradation:
- Replica autoscaling: horizontal scaling at 65% GPU utilization target; when utilization exceeds 90% we enact soft-throttling (shed low-priority requests) and route to a lower-cost model variant that is compatible with the API. Failover to a lower-accuracy quantized model is configurable and recorded as part of our SLA exception latency logs.
- Fallback behavior: 1) intra-region model variant fallback (same family, different quantization), 2) cross-region fallback (higher-latency), 3) queued backpressure with priority lanes. Each fallback path is logged and contributes to an SLA exception event.

Artifacts included in inference_test_plan.md (attached):
- exact k6 scenario configs and open-source feeder script
- priming script used to seed KV caches
- replica/worker sizing matrix and expected batch distributions
- post-processing scripts used to derive p50/p95/p99 from raw token timestamps

CSV outputs in redwood_perf_evidence_v1.tar.gz: raw token timestamps, per-request end-to-end latencies, batch sizes per infer call, and observed GPU utilization traces. The latency matrix (redwood_latency_matrix.csv) maps workload profile x replica count -> p50/p95/p99.

Security/multi-tenant isolation notes:
- Hosted tenants operate on isolated process sandboxes with GPU scheduling groups. Cold-starts may be multiplexed across nodes depending on your plan; Dedicated offers strict host-reservation.
- During noisy-neighbor bursts we measure degradation primarily via increased batch sizes and slightly elevated p95; our model routing will shift non-critical requests to slower variants to preserve critical request latency SLOs. We include a documented experiment where we introduced a synthetic noisy tenant at 10x baseline for 30 minutes and measured the impact — results are in the CSV.

Let me know if you want us to re-run any profile at a different token length or to include tool-call latencies end-to-end (we can stitch in external API timing from an instrumented client).

—Jonas
Jonas Weber
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Jones <alex.jones@peregrinehealth.com>
Cc: Hannah Schmitt <hannah.schmitt@redwood.ai>, Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-07-27T11:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: RFP - Appendix C: performance test clarifications

Alex — adding the raw evidence set and a quick interpretation guide. Quick highlights from our runs (long-form profile unless noted):

- At 250 QPS (4 replicas), p50 = 38ms, p95 = 122ms, p99 = 310ms (token-gen latency). Batch sizes averaged 3.6 tokens per infer call; GPU util ~72% steady.
- At 1k QPS (16 replicas), p50 = 44ms, p95 = 140ms, p99 = 420ms; batch size increased to 6.1 tokens per infer call (more efficient throughput).
- Cold-start: average model load time 18.5 s (container + weights), median model warmup priming 90s to reach steady-state batch distribution.
- Noisy-neighbor experiment: injected 8x burst on co-located tenant for 15 minutes — observed p95 increase to 210ms for affected tenant; fallback rules reduced impact for high-priority traffic to p95=130ms by routing low-priority requests to quantized variant.

Notes on reproducing the CSVs: open the CSVs in the tarball and run the 'derive_summary.py' script to regenerate the percentile rows. The file redwood_latency_matrix.csv is intended to be a short digest you can paste into the vendor packet.

Drive link for artifacts (read-only): https://drive.redwood.ai/teams/perf/peregrine-evidence
HubSpot record (internal): https://hubspot.redwood.ai/deals/DEAL-7931

If you want, we can provide a stripped-down k6 profile and a reproducible GCP/EC2 notebook to run a compatible test in your environment.

—Marissa
Marissa Cole
Principal Performance Engineer
Redwood Inference
